title: Optimizing road side units connectivity in intelligent transportation systems with optical network solutions
text:
We have just published a new paper:





Citation: Camilo Anzola-Rojas, Ignacio de Miguel, Noemí Merayo, Juan Carlos Aguado, Rubén M. Lorenzo, Ramón J. Durán Barroso, Optimizing road side units connectivity in intelligent transportation systems with optical network solutions, Vehicular Communications, Volume 56, 2025, 100975, ISSN 2214-2096, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.vehcom.2025.100975. (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2214209625001020)


Abstract: A fundamental component of Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) is connectivity. For connected vehicles to be aware of events occurring nearby, or even far from them, roadside infrastructure is essential. Roadside Units (RSUs) are electronic equipment placed along highways to provide connectivity and share data with vehicles, other RSUs, and networks. Connected vehicles require wireless communication with RSUs; however, depending on the complexity of tasks and the number of users, spectrum resources may be insufficient to handle all required communication between vehicles, RSUs and external networks. Since RSUs are stationary, optical fiber is an ideal technology for interconnecting them and linking them to the Internet and the cloud, providing reliable, high-performance connectivity, with low signal attenuation and high bandwidth. This paper proposes a model for deploying fiber networks to connect RSUs, with a focus on minimizing capital expenditures, including costs for civil works, cables, and devices, which are critical considerations given the large distances involved. Specifically, we consider and compare two established optical network technologies: point-to-point (PtP) and passive optical networks (PON). To support this comparison, we present and test two novel Integer Linear Programming (ILP) formulations: one for PtP and one for PON. Additionally, we introduce a genetic algorithm that improves upon a previously proposed heuristic, achieving near-optimal results comparable to the ILP formulation, while efficiently solving large-scale scenarios. The results show that the optimal choice between PtP and PON depends on the deployment area and density of RSUs. Keywords: Networks; Optical fiber; Passive optical networks; Roadside units; Vehicles; Communications
Funding: This work was supported by Ministerio de Ciencia, Innovación y Universidades / Agencia Estatal de Investigación (Grants PID2023-148104OB-C41 and PID2020-112675RB-C42 funded by MICIU/AEI/10.13039/501100011033 and the former also by ERFD/EU, European Regional Development Fund/European Union)

title: About GCO
text:
The Optical Communications Group (GCO) at Universidad de Valladolid has carried out, since its creation, extensive activity in the field of basic research on optical components, later expanding into the design of optical networks, and more recently addressing other areas such as radio communications, vehicular communications and wireless localization systems. Thus, new lines of work have progressively opened in various areas.
The group currently works in five core areas: optical communication networks, vehicular communications, radio communications, rehabilitation technologies, and educational innovation. In this regard, the group has always been concerned with researching improvements in teaching–learning processes, developing various projects focused on educational support software and the improvement of teaching materials.
Contact: Prof. Evaristo J. Abril: ejabril@tel.uva.es

title: About GCO
text:
The group started working on the field of optical components and their applications. Then, at the end of 1998 a new research line was launched, focused on the analysis and design of optical networks. Given the group’s experience in components, the initial research concentrated on analyzing the optimal placement of components in the network. Later, the research centered on the design and optimization of WRONs (Wavelength-Routed Optical Networks). In this field, the group has proposed several efficient and fast algorithms for designing virtual topologies, new methods for solving the static routing and wavelength assignment (RWA) problem, and metaheuristic techniques such as ant colony optimization and genetic algorithms for solving both static and dynamic RWA problems. These techniques have been shown to deliver excellent results with significantly lower computation time compared to other alternatives. More recently, the group has developed genetic-algorithm-based methods for designing logical topologies in reconfigurable WDM networks and for the routing and dimensioning of networks. Work has also been conducted on hybrid networks, proposing polymorphic networks in collaboration with the Electro-Optical Communications Group at Eindhoven University of Technology (TU/e). This type of network combines several switching paradigms within a single physical network, ensuring that each service uses the most suitable paradigm.
As part of the FP7 CHRON project, which the group coordinated, the concept of CHRON Networks (Cognitive and Heterogeneous Reconfigurable Optical Networks) was proposed. In this area, the group has explored the use of cognitive methods for the control and design of these networks. Within the broader field of Artificial Intelligence, the group has collaborated with the Research Group of Admela Jukan (currently at the Technische Universität Braunschweig), with whom a recent survey article on the use of AI in optical networks was published. More recently, research has begun on the design of control algorithms for elastic or flexible optical networks. Thanks to collaboration with Telefónica I+D, the group has worked on evaluating the impact of the TCP protocol on Optical Burst Switching (OBS) networks.
Another line of research focuses on proposing medium access control mechanisms for passive optical access networks that can provide adequate Quality of Service (QoS) according to stipulated requirements and user differentiation aligned with service provider conditions. Several methods and algorithms have been proposed for managing EPON and GPON access networks, as well as Long-Reach PON networks. Part of this work has resulted in collaborations and publications with Professor John Senior’s Group at the University of Hertfordshire and with the Telecommunication Networks Engineering Group (GIRTEL) at the University of Cartagena. In addition, a research line centered on Software Defined Networks (SDN) is starting within the area of passive optical access networks, using a 25-kilometer real GPON testbed built in the group’s laboratory. Part of this work is being carried out in collaboration with the Polytechnic University of Madrid (UPM) and has already produced recent publications.
In recent years a new research topic has opened related to radio communications, dosimetry, and localization. This includes several lines of work: one focusing on the integration of measurement station systems, another on MIMO systems, and a third on indoor wireless localization techniques. The group is also now working on solving intermediate-frequency regime problems in the fields of dosimetry and localization.
The Optical Communications Group also works on a consolidated research line that develops prototypes for Rehabilitation Technologies. This includes the implementation of real-time systems for the extraction, processing, and interpretation of biomedical signals, as well as systems for sensory or functional stimulation for users with various conditions.
Members of the group participate in several scientific and professional societies—IEEE, OSA (now Optica), and COIT/AEIT—and serve as reviewers for numerous international publications in the field of optical communications, including Electronics Letters, Photonics Technology Letters, Optics Letters, Optics Communications, Journal of the Optical Society of America B, IEEE/OSA Journal of Lightwave Technology, IEEE/OSA Journal of Optical Communications and Networking, and Elsevier Optical Switching and Networking. The group’s work in supervising doctoral theses and final degree projects has been recognized with several national, regional, and local awards.

title: Innovation on Education
text:
Overview
The objective of this line of research in the coming years will focus on virtual teaching and interaction with e-learning and m-learning telematic tools, as these have become an essential support for new teaching methodologies due to their flexibility, development and the degree of attraction and dynamism they offer in the teaching-learning process. In this regard, the Optical Communications Group at the University of Valladolid is immersed in the design and development of different tools and applications with these characteristics.
On the one hand, the GCO has developed a virtual learning environment called AIM-Mobile Learning Platform, winner of the First Prize of the Social Council of the University of Valladolid (UVA) in 2015, which aims to enhance teacher-student interaction, streamline and automate certain educational tasks such as continuous assessment in the classroom in real time, as well as the design of interactive online resources and content and the management of students, teachers and subjects, all through mobile and wireless devices. This environment is multifunctional, consisting of a server application (used by the teacher) and a client application (used by the student). The learning environment is directly applicable in multidisciplinary educational contexts and is available in several languages, with the first experimental prototype being used in subjects from different degree programmes. However, work continues to promote and encourage the continued use of the virtual environment, implementing and integrating new features and improvements that meet the objectives of the teaching-learning process. In addition, the GCO has also developed applications for Android tablets/mobile phones to support teachers in monitoring students’ work and facilitating continuous assessment.
